# Submarine and torpedo (`submarine_torpedo`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: needs buoyancy_hydrostatics; helped by internal_combustion_engine, dynamo_electric_motor, electric_battery, steamship_screw_propeller
- Core idea: A sealed hull dives by letting water into ballast tanks until it weighs as much as the water it displaces, steers in depth with horizontal rudders, and surfaces by blowing the tanks with compressed air. It needs an engine that uses no air under water, which in practice meant electric motors on batteries charged by a combustion engine at the surface. Its weapon is the torpedo, a small self-propelled craft that holds a set depth by a pressure sensor and pendulum and strikes below the waterline. Cheap submarines can sink the merchant ships a sea power lives on; the answer was to sail merchant ships in escorted convoys.
- Pitfalls:
  - Neutral buoyancy is unstable; without depth rudders and trim tanks the boat either pops up or keeps sinking
  - Air for the crew and exhaust for any engine; hand-cranked boats suffocated or exhausted their crews
  - Before 1866 'torpedo' meant a mine or a charge on a pole, Hunley was lost after its attack in 1864, and the cause remains disputed
  - Hunting submarines with patrols instead of convoying the targets; Britain nearly lost the war that way in early 1917
- History: europe: c. 1620–1624 – Drebbel's oared submersible on the Thames; 1866 – Whitehead's self-propelled torpedo at Fiume (Rijeka); 1915–1918 – German U-boat campaigns; 1917 – convoy system; americas: 1776 – Bushnell's Turtle; 1864 – H. L. Hunley sinks USS Housatonic and is lost; 1897–1900 – John Holland's petrol-electric boat, accepted by the US Navy
- Read:
  - Edwyn Gray, The Devil's Device: The Story of Robert Whitehead, Inventor of the Torpedo (1975)
  - Richard Compton-Hall, Submarine Boats: The Beginnings of Underwater Warfare (1983)
